messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Marsh is a 73-year-old divorced journalist who spent the better part of four decades covering industrial and environmental catastrophes across North America. He came to his first intake appointment wearing a pressed oxford shirt and carrying a reporter's notebook out of what appeared to be old habit, though he admitted he had not written a publishable word in nearly two years. He sat down only after positioning his chair so that his back was flush against the wall of the consulting room, scanning the space briefly before settling. He did not appear to notice he had done it.

Approximately twenty-six months before seeking treatment, Gerald was embedded with a response team during a catastrophic chemical plant explosion in the Gulf Coast region — an event he had arranged access to through contacts cultivated over a long career. He arrived on-site expecting the controlled aftermath typical of industrial incidents. What he encountered instead was ongoing, cascading failure: secondary explosions, the collapse of a storage structure while workers were still inside, and the release of a dense chemical plume that moved faster than anyone had predicted. Gerald was in a press staging area when the second explosion occurred without warning. The concussive force knocked him from his feet. In the chaos that followed, he lay partially pinned beneath debris for approximately forty minutes, unable to move, surrounded by the screams of injured workers and the acrid, sweetish chemical smell that had saturated the air and coated the back of his throat. It was a taste unlike anything he had encountered before — viscous, almost metallic beneath its sweetness — and it stayed with him long after the physical exposure had passed.

In the weeks following his evacuation and medical clearance, Gerald found himself unable to file his account of the event. He told his editor it was a question of verification. He told himself the same thing. What was actually happening was that any attempt to sit with the material — reviewing photographs from the scene, reading wire copy from other outlets — produced a quality of experience he struggled to articulate: the memory did not feel like remembering. It felt like being returned. The images played with a continuity and physical immediacy that made the present room dissolve. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself to go there fully, something in him would not come back intact.

The unpredictability of the second explosion had lodged itself as a permanent feature of his world. Gerald had always prided himself on reading situations, on knowing where the danger was. Now he understood, in a way that felt cellular rather than intellectual, that danger did not announce itself. In restaurants and waiting rooms and the lobby of his apartment building, he began cataloguing exits, noting the weight and reach of objects near other people's hands — a habit he was certain was simply reasonable given what he now knew. He listened each night for sounds at his front door. He could not remember the last time his body had felt at rest.

His spending had escalated quietly. Small purchases at first — books he did not read, equipment for a kitchen he barely used — then larger ones, a pattern he recognised intellectually as purposeless but that provided, in the moment of transaction, a few minutes of something that approximated relief. His ex-wife, with whom he had maintained a cordial post-divorce friendship for nearly a decade, had stopped calling after he cancelled three consecutive plans without explanation. He had not tried to repair it. The effort required felt disproportionate to what he believed he could offer anyone.

What finally brought Gerald in was a dinner with a former colleague at which a dish arrived that carried, faintly but unmistakably, that same sweetish chemical undertone — likely nothing more than a particular reduction sauce. He froze completely, fork in hand, unable to speak or move for what his colleague later told him was nearly a full minute. He drove home and sat in his car in the parking garage for two hours. He had come to believe he would never feel anything the way he used to — not curiosity, not pleasure, not the particular satisfaction that had once made the work feel worth the cost. He was not certain therapy could return any of that. What he said, quietly, at the end of the intake session, was that he wanted to find out whether it was still possible to live in the present tense.
